To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the performance of recommenders is not constant across all items and users; (2) the performance of individual recommenders is correlated with the performance of other recommenders; (3) the correlation between recommenders can be used to predict when recommenders will fail; and (4) these correlations can be used in hybridization to improve recommendation quality.

1) there is a strong correlation between the ratings given to a movie and the ratings given to the movies that the user also rated; 2) the correlation between ratings given to a user and ratings given to the users the user also rated is weaker, but still significant; and 3) the correlation between a movie and the movies it co-occurred with in ratings is very weak.

(1) the performance of recommenders on a particular user-item pair varies widely, (2) the performance of a recommender on a particular user can be predicted from the performance of that recommender on the same user-item pairs for a different item, (3) the performance of an algorithm for a particular user-item combination can be predicted from its performance on the same user for a different item.

the failure modes of recommenders are not random, and that we can predict these failure modes with reasonable success.

recommender failures are not random but can be predicted.
there are many cases in which a recommender algorithm fails, but that the failure can be predicted by another recommender algorithm.

the failure of one algorithm does not necessarily mean that all algorithms are likely to fail on a given item, and thus that a simple majority vote of the component algorithms may be an effective way to combine them.
